check.q: Which part moves the fabric forward under the needle?
check.why: The feed dogs are the teeth under the presser foot; they grip the fabric and move it forward one stitch at a time.

check.q: Which direction do you turn the hand wheel?
choices: Either way, it does not matter
Only while the pedal is pressed
check.why: The hand wheel always turns toward you. Turning it away can pull the thread out of the needle and cause a jam.

check.q: A student wants to sew slowly while learning. What controls the speed?
choices: How hard the foot pedal is pressed
check.why: The foot pedal works like a gas pedal. Light pressure sews slowly; more pressure sews faster.

lessons.title: Needle Types and Sizes
lessons.mainIdea: The needle must match the fabric: a ballpoint for knits, a universal for most wovens, a heavy needle for denim, and a fresh one for every project.
reading: Look closely at a machine needle. It has a flat side on the shank at the top, a long groove down the front, a scarf (a scooped-out spot) on the back just above the eye, and a point. The flat side faces the back of the machine on most home machines, so the needle can only go in one way. The eye is near the point, not at the top like a hand needle, because the machine pushes the thread down through the fabric instead of pulling it.

Needles come in types by point shape. A *universal* needle has a slightly rounded point and handles most woven cottons and blends. A *ballpoint* needle has a rounder tip that slides between the loops of a knit fabric instead of piercing and cutting them; use it for T-shirt jersey and fleece. A stretch needle is for very stretchy fabric like swimwear. A denim or jeans needle has a strong, sharp point for thick layers. A microtex or sharp needle makes a fine straight hole in silky fabric.

Needles also come in sizes, written as two numbers such as 80/12 or 90/14. The first number is the European size and the second the American; both get bigger as the needle gets thicker. A 70/10 suits light cotton, an 80/12 is the everyday size for medium fabric, and a 100/16 handles denim. A needle that is too thin for the fabric bends and breaks; one that is too thick leaves visible holes.

Needles dull with use, and a dull needle skips stitches and punches instead of piercing. Many sewers change the needle at the start of every project or after about eight hours of sewing. To change it, turn the machine off, loosen the needle clamp screw, pull the old needle down and out, push the new one up as far as it will go with the flat side to the back, and tighten the screw. Drop the old needle into a lidded container, never a bare trash can.

words.d: a machine needle with a slightly rounded point that suits most woven fabrics
a needle with a rounded tip that slips between knit loops instead of cutting them
the thickness of a needle, written as two numbers such as 80/12; bigger numbers are thicker
the scooped-out spot on the back of a machine needle above the eye, where the hook catches the thread

look.title: Common Needle Sizes and Their Fabrics (a typical guide)
look.cite: typical home-sewing needle guide; check your machine manual and needle package
look.prompt: A student has heavy denim and only a 70/10 needle. What is likely to happen, and what size should they get?

check.q: Which needle should you use for a stretchy T-shirt knit?
check.why: A ballpoint needle slides between knit loops instead of cutting them, so the fabric does not get runs or holes.

check.q: What does a bigger needle number, like 100/16 instead of 70/10, mean?
check.why: Both numbers grow as the needle gets thicker. A 100/16 is a heavy needle for denim; a 70/10 is thin, for light fabric.

check.q: When you insert a new needle on a home machine, which way does the flat side of the shank face?
choices: Toward the back of the machine
check.why: The flat side faces the back on most home machines, so the needle seats correctly and the scarf faces the hook.

lessons.title: Reading the Manual
lessons.mainIdea: Every machine is a little different, and the manual is where the threading diagram, the bobbin type and the needle position for your machine actually live.
reading: Two machines side by side in a classroom can thread differently, take different bobbins and put the stitch length on a different dial. That is why the first tool for any machine is its *manual*. If the paper copy is lost, the model number is printed on a plate on the back or bottom of the machine, and the maker usually posts the manual online for free. Print the threading diagram and tape it to the table.

Open the manual and find four things before you sew. First, the threading diagram, drawn as numbered arrows from the spool to the needle. Second, the bobbin section: does the machine take a drop-in bobbin from the top, or a front-loading bobbin in a metal *bobbin case*? Third, the needle-threading direction: front to back on most machines, but some thread side to side. Fourth, the normal tension setting, often 4 on a dial that runs 0 to 9.

The manual also has a troubleshooting table near the back. It lists the problem in one column (thread breaks, fabric will not feed, skipped stitches) and the likely causes in the other. Almost every cause is one of four things: threading, needle, bobbin, or lint. Read that table once now, so that when the machine acts up, you know the list exists.

Class machines get shared, so the manual is also the record of what the machine can do. Note the stitches it offers, the widest zigzag it can make, and what presser feet came with it. A zipper foot or a buttonhole foot in the accessory box is useless if nobody knows it is there.

words.d: the maker's booklet for one model of machine, with its threading diagram and troubleshooting table
the small metal holder a bobbin sits in on a front-loading machine; it sets the bobbin thread tension
a bobbin that sits in a clear-lidded well on top of the machine bed, in front of the needle

look.title: Four Machines, Four Answers
look.text: Machine A: front-loading bobbin case, threads front to back. Machine B: drop-in bobbin, threads front to back. Machine C: drop-in bobbin, threads left to right. Machine D: front-loading, tension dial normal at 3 instead of 4. A student who learned on Machine B sits down at Machine C and threads the needle front to back.
look.prompt: What will happen on Machine C, and what one page of the manual would have prevented it?

check.q: Where is the model number of a sewing machine usually found?
choices: On a plate on the back or bottom of the machine
check.why: The model plate is on the back or underside. With the model number you can find the manual online.

check.q: Which part of the manual should you check when the thread keeps breaking?
check.why: The troubleshooting table lists each problem with its likely causes, which are usually threading, needle, bobbin or lint.

check.q: A machine's bobbin sits under a clear lid in front of the needle. What kind of bobbin system is that?
check.why: A drop-in bobbin sits in a well on top of the bed under a clear plate. Front-loading bobbins go in a metal case behind a door.

lessons.title: The Top Thread Path
lessons.mainIdea: The top thread follows one fixed path from spool to needle, and it only works if the presser foot is up when you thread it.
reading: Turn the machine off. Raise the presser foot with the lever behind it. This matters more than any other step: raising the foot opens the tension discs so the thread can slip between them. Turn the hand wheel toward you until the take-up lever is at its highest point, where you can see it through the slot. Now put the spool on the spool pin with the thread coming off in the direction the manual shows, and cap it with the spool holder if the machine has one.

Pull the thread to the left along the top of the machine and into the first thread guide. Bring it down the front channel, around the bottom, and back up. On the way down it passes between the tension discs; you may feel a tiny click as it seats. At the top of the channel it goes right to left through the eye of the take-up lever. If you miss the take-up lever, every stitch will be loose. Then bring it straight down through the lower thread guides to the needle.

Thread the needle from front to back on most machines, and pull about six inches of thread out behind the presser foot. Many machines have a built-in needle threader: a tiny hook that swings through the eye, catches the thread, and pulls it back through. Now lower the presser foot. Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you, and the needle thread will catch the bobbin thread and pull a loop of it up through the throat plate.

Check your work with a tug test. With the presser foot up, the thread should pull freely. Lower the foot and pull again; there should be firm drag. If it pulls freely with the foot down, the thread is not between the discs. Pull it out and rethread. Threading takes thirty seconds when it becomes a habit, and it prevents most of the jams a beginner ever sees.

words.d: two metal plates that pinch the top thread; the presser foot lever opens them for threading
a hook or slot that holds the thread on its path between the spool and the needle
a small built-in hook that pushes through the needle eye, catches the thread and pulls it back

look.title: Put the Path in Order
look.text: Six steps, out of order: (a) through the eye of the take-up lever; (b) raise the presser foot and put the take-up lever at its highest point; (c) through the needle eye, front to back; (d) into the first thread guide on top; (e) down between the tension discs; (f) spool on the spool pin.
look.prompt: Write the letters in the right order, and say which single step, if skipped, leaves the thread with no tension at all.

check.q: Why must the presser foot be UP when you thread the top of the machine?
choices: So the needle can move freely
So the tension discs open and the thread can seat between them
So the bobbin can drop in
check.why: Raising the presser foot opens the tension discs. With the foot down the discs are closed and the thread lies on top of them with no tension.

check.q: A seam has good stitches for two inches and then every stitch is loose. The student threaded the machine with the foot up, but skipped one part. Which part?
check.why: The take-up lever pulls each stitch tight. If the thread is not through its eye, the stitches stay loose.

check.q: What does a correct tug test feel like with the presser foot down?
choices: The thread pulls freely with no drag
The thread will not move at all
The thread pulls with firm, even drag
check.why: With the foot down the discs are closed, so a correctly seated thread pulls with steady drag. Free pulling means it missed the discs.

lessons.title: Winding a Bobbin
lessons.mainIdea: A bobbin must be wound evenly, at a steady speed, with the same thread as the top, or the stitch underneath will never be right.
reading: A *bobbin* is a small flat spool that holds the bottom thread. Use an empty bobbin made for your machine; bobbins look alike but differ by a millimeter, and the wrong one jams or rattles. Use the same thread as the top for ordinary seams. Put the spool on the spool pin, run the thread through the bobbin winder guide (often a small disc on top of the machine), and pass the end through the hole in the bobbin from the inside out.

Push the bobbin onto the bobbin winder spindle and click the spindle to the right, which disengages the needle so it will not move while you wind. On older machines you loosen the hand wheel's inner knob instead. Hold the thread tail up, press the pedal slowly for a few turns so the thread catches, stop, and trim the tail close to the bobbin. Then press the pedal at a steady, medium speed and let the machine fill the bobbin. Most machines stop by themselves when it is full.

Watch the bobbin as it fills. The thread should lie in smooth, even layers. If it piles up on one side, the thread is not through the winder guide correctly; stop and fix it. Do not overfill; thread should not bulge past the rim. Cut the thread, click the spindle back to the left, and the needle is connected again. Turn the hand wheel a half turn to make sure.

Two common mistakes: winding on top of thread already on the bobbin, which makes uneven tension and a bird's nest underneath, and winding at a jerky speed, which stretches some layers tighter than others. Keep a few extra bobbins wound in the colors you use most; running out mid-seam is a nuisance, not a disaster, but it always happens at the worst moment.

words.d: the small flat spool under the throat plate that supplies the bottom thread of every stitch
the spindle on top of the machine that spins an empty bobbin to fill it with thread
a tangle of loose thread under the fabric, usually from threading or bobbin mistakes

look.title: A Bobbin That Looks Wrong
look.text: A student holds up a freshly wound bobbin. The thread is piled high on the left rim and thin on the right, and there is a loose loop hanging off. Under the new thread you can see a layer of blue thread from last week. The student says it will probably work.
look.prompt: Name the two winding mistakes you can see, and say what each one will do to the stitch on the underside of the fabric.

check.q: Before winding a bobbin, why do you click the winder spindle to the right?
choices: To disengage the needle so it does not move while you wind
check.why: Moving the spindle into winding position disconnects the needle. Otherwise the needle stitches away while you wind.

check.q: A wound bobbin has thread piled on one side and thin on the other. What went wrong?
choices: The thread was not seated in the winder guide
The pedal was pressed too softly
check.why: The winder guide feeds the thread onto the bobbin evenly. If the thread misses it, the layers pile up unevenly.

check.q: What is the safest rule about the bobbin you choose?
choices: Use the biggest one that fits
Use the bobbin made for your machine model
Use a metal bobbin in every machine
check.why: Bobbins differ by a millimeter or so between models. A wrong-size bobbin rattles, jams or throws the tension off.

lessons.title: Inserting the Bobbin
lessons.mainIdea: The bobbin must sit in its case or well with the thread coming off in the direction the manual shows, then be pulled through its own tension spring and up through the plate.
reading: There are two systems. For a *drop-in* machine, slide off the clear cover in front of the needle. Hold the bobbin so the thread comes off in the direction the diagram on the cover shows, usually counterclockwise, like a letter P when you look at it. Drop it into the well, then pull the thread tail into the slot and along the guide path marked by arrows, which slides it under a small tension spring. Leave a few inches of tail and replace the cover.

For a *front-loading* machine, open the door below the needle and pull out the bobbin case by its little hinged latch. Hold the case in your left hand with the open side up and drop the bobbin in so the thread comes off in the direction the manual shows. Pull the thread into the slit on the side of the case and under the flat tension spring until it clicks out the end. Hold the latch open, push the case onto the center pin until it clicks, and let go of the latch.

Now bring the bobbin thread up. Hold the top thread loosely in your left hand. Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you. The needle goes down, catches the bobbin thread and lifts a loop of it. Tug the top thread and the loop comes through the hole in the throat plate. Pull both tails out and lay them back under the presser foot, toward the rear. Starting a seam with the tails held behind the foot stops the first stitch from pulling down into the plate.

If the bobbin is put in backward, the thread unwinds the wrong way against its spring and the bottom stitches come out loose or the thread breaks. If the thread never went under the bobbin tension spring, there is no bottom tension at all, and loops of top thread show on the underside. Both look like tension problems. Both are really bobbin problems, and both take twenty seconds to fix.

words.d: a bobbin system where the bobbin drops into a well on top of the bed under a clear cover
a bobbin system where the bobbin sits in a removable metal case behind a door below the needle
the flat spring on the bobbin case or well that the bottom thread must pass under to get its tension

look.title: Two Bobbins, One Right
look.text: Two drop-in machines sit side by side. In machine one the bobbin thread comes off counterclockwise, matching the arrow on the cover, and runs through the slot under the spring. In machine two the bobbin was dropped in flipped over, so the thread comes off clockwise, and the tail was left lying loose on top of the bobbin.
look.prompt: Predict what the underside of the first seam will look like on machine two, and list the two fixes in order.

check.q: After dropping in the bobbin, why do you pull the thread through the slot along the arrows?
choices: To seat the thread under the bobbin tension spring
check.why: The slot guides the thread under the bobbin's flat tension spring. Without that, the bottom thread has no tension.

check.q: How do you bring the bobbin thread up through the throat plate?
choices: Turn the hand wheel one full turn toward you while holding the top thread
Pull it up with tweezers through the needle hole
Wind the bobbin with the cover off
check.why: One turn of the hand wheel sends the needle down to catch the bobbin thread and lift a loop. A tug on the top thread pulls it through.

check.q: Where should both thread tails be before you start sewing?
choices: Pulled back under and behind the presser foot
Cut off flush with the plate
check.why: Tails laid toward the rear under the foot stop the first stitch from pulling the thread down into the plate.

lessons.title: The Lockstitch, Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: A lockstitch forms when the needle carries the top thread down, a hook loops it around the bobbin thread, and the take-up lever pulls the two threads tight so they lock inside the fabric.
reading: A home sewing machine makes a *lockstitch*. It is nothing like hand sewing, where one thread goes in and out. Here two threads never actually pass through each other's spools; they twist around each other once per stitch and lock in the middle of the fabric. Turn the hand wheel slowly toward you with the bobbin cover off and you can watch the whole thing happen.

Step one: the needle pushes the top thread down through the fabric and through the hole in the throat plate. Step two: the needle starts back up. Because the thread drags a little against the fabric, a small loop of top thread bulges out on the scarf side of the needle. Step three: the *hook*, a curved metal point spinning around the bobbin, catches that loop and carries it all the way around the bobbin case, so the loop now wraps around the bobbin thread.

Step four: the take-up lever rises fast and yanks the slack out of the top thread. That pulls the twist of the two threads up into the layers of fabric. At the same time the feed dogs push the fabric forward one stitch length. Step five: the needle comes down again and the cycle repeats. A machine at full speed can do this several hundred times a minute, and each stitch is locked by the one before it.

This is why the scarf on the needle matters and why the needle must be in the right way around: the hook has to pass right behind the eye to catch the loop. It is also why a bent or dull needle skips stitches. If the loop forms in the wrong place, the hook misses it, and no stitch forms for that beat. Understanding the cycle turns most machine problems from mysteries into checklists.

words.d: the machine stitch made by the top thread looping around the bobbin thread and locking in the fabric
the curved point that spins around the bobbin and catches the loop of top thread on each stitch
a beat where the hook misses the loop and no stitch forms, leaving a long gap in the seam

look.title: Watch One Stitch Form
look.text: With the bobbin cover off, a student turns the hand wheel toward herself very slowly and describes what she sees: the needle goes down through a scrap. As it starts to rise, a small loop of thread bulges out behind the needle. A curved point sweeps past and takes the loop around the bobbin. Then the arm at the top jerks up and the loop disappears into the fabric.
look.prompt: Name the part doing the work at each of the four moments, and explain why turning the wheel away from her would break the cycle.

check.q: Which part catches the loop of top thread and carries it around the bobbin?
check.why: The hook is the curved point that spins around the bobbin. It catches the loop that forms behind the rising needle.

check.q: What does the take-up lever do right after the loop goes around the bobbin?
choices: Pulls the slack out so the two threads lock inside the fabric
check.why: The take-up lever rises and pulls the top thread tight, drawing the twist of the two threads up into the fabric layers.

check.q: Why does a bent needle cause skipped stitches?
choices: The loop forms in the wrong place and the hook misses it
check.why: The hook must pass right behind the needle's scarf to catch the loop. A bent needle puts the loop out of reach.

lessons.title: Stitch Length and Width
lessons.mainIdea: Stitch length sets how far the fabric moves per stitch and width sets how far the needle swings sideways; 2.5 mm straight is the everyday setting.
reading: The *stitch length* dial controls the feed dogs. A higher number moves the fabric farther between needle strikes, so each stitch is longer. Most machines mark length in millimeters, from 0 to 4 or 5. Some older machines use stitches per inch instead, where a bigger number means shorter stitches. For ordinary seams in medium fabric, set 2.5 mm, which is about 10 to 12 stitches per inch. Set the dial before you sew; changing it mid-seam leaves a visible step in the stitching.

Use a long stitch, 4 to 5 mm, for *basting*: a temporary seam you will pull out later, or gathering, where you pull the bobbin thread to draw the fabric up into small folds. Long stitches are easy to remove. Use a shorter stitch, about 2 mm, for lightweight fabric and curves, where short stitches follow the shape better. Very short stitches, under 1 mm, are hard to rip out and can chew the fabric.

The *stitch width* dial controls how far the needle swings from side to side. On a straight stitch the width is zero and the needle goes straight up and down. Turn the width up and the machine sews a *zigzag*. A width of about 3 mm with a length of 2 mm gives a medium zigzag good for finishing a raw edge. A wide, very short zigzag becomes a satin stitch, the dense band used on appliqué and buttonholes.

Test every setting on a scrap of the same fabric first, doubled the way the seam will be. The scrap shows you whether the stitches lie flat, whether the fabric puckers, and whether the length looks right. Write the setting that worked on a sticky note and keep it with the project. A machine that is set right for one fabric is rarely right for the next.

words.d: how far the feed dogs move the fabric between stitches, usually in millimeters; 2.5 mm is standard
how far the needle swings sideways; zero for a straight stitch, more for zigzag
a temporary seam sewn with a long stitch, 4 to 5 mm, so it pulls out easily
a stitch where the needle swings side to side; used to finish edges and sew stretch seams

look.title: Stitch Length by Job (typical settings)
look.cite: typical home-machine settings; the machine manual and a test scrap decide the final number
look.prompt: A student basted a sleeve at 2.0 mm and now has to remove it. What went wrong, and which row should they have used?

check.q: What is a good stitch length for an ordinary seam in medium-weight cotton?
check.why: 2.5 mm, about 10 to 12 stitches per inch, is the everyday setting. Longer is for basting; much shorter is for dense stitching.

check.q: You need to gather a ruffle by pulling the bobbin thread. Which stitch length do you set?
check.why: Long stitches slide easily along the fabric when you pull the bobbin thread, and they pull out cleanly afterward.

check.q: Which dial do you turn to change a straight stitch into a zigzag?
check.why: Width controls the needle's side-to-side swing. At zero the needle goes straight; turning it up makes a zigzag.

lessons.title: Reading the Tension
lessons.mainIdea: A balanced stitch locks in the middle of the fabric; loops on the bottom mean the top is too loose, and bobbin thread showing on top means the top is too tight.
reading: *Tension* is how hard each thread is held back as it feeds. The top thread's tension comes from the discs and the dial; the bobbin thread's comes from the small spring on the case or well. When the two match, the twist where the threads lock sits in the middle of the fabric layers, and the seam looks the same on both sides. To learn to read tension, sew a test line with a different color in the bobbin than on top.

Look at the underside. If you see loops or straight runs of the top color lying on the bottom, the top thread is too *loose*: it is being pulled all the way through to the underside. Turn the top tension dial to a higher number, one step at a time, and test again. If instead the bobbin color shows in dots along the top of the seam, the top thread is too *tight*: it is dragging the bobbin thread up. Turn the dial to a lower number.

Before you touch the dial, though, check the path. In most classrooms, nine out of ten "tension problems" are a top thread that missed the discs or the take-up lever, a bobbin inserted backward, or a bobbin thread that never went under its spring. Rethread top and bobbin with the presser foot up and test again. Only if a correctly threaded machine still stitches unevenly do you change the dial. Adjusting the bobbin spring is a last resort and is usually a teacher's job.

Some fabrics need a small change: thick layers may want slightly higher top tension, and very fine fabric slightly lower. Write down the dial number that gives a balanced stitch for each fabric, and always put the dial back to its normal setting, usually about 4, before you leave the machine for the next person.

words.d: how firmly the thread is held back as it feeds; top tension is set by the dial, bottom by the bobbin spring
a stitch where the two threads lock in the middle of the fabric and both sides look the same
too little top tension: the top thread shows as loops on the underside of the fabric
too much top tension: the bobbin thread is pulled up and shows as dots on the top side

look.title: Diagnose Three Seams
look.text: Three test seams, each sewn with red thread on top and blue in the bobbin. Seam 1: both sides show only their own color, flat and even. Seam 2: the underside has long red loops and the fabric puckers slightly. Seam 3: the top side shows a row of tiny blue dots, and the seam feels stiff and drawn up.
look.prompt: Say which seam is balanced, which is too loose on top, and which is too tight, and give the first thing to check for seams 2 and 3 before turning any dial.

check.q: Loops of top thread show on the underside of a seam. What does that tell you?
choices: The top thread is too loose
The top thread is too tight
check.why: When the top thread is pulled all the way through to the bottom and shows as loops, the top tension is too low (or the thread missed the discs).

check.q: What is the FIRST thing to do when a seam looks like a tension problem?
choices: Rethread top and bobbin with the presser foot up
check.why: Most tension symptoms are threading errors. Rethreading fixes them; the dial only matters once the path is right.

check.q: Dots of bobbin thread show on the top side of the seam. Which way do you turn the top tension dial?
choices: Lower, to loosen the top thread
Leave it; the bobbin is the problem
check.why: Bobbin thread on top means the top is pulling too hard. Lowering the top tension one step at a time brings the lock back to the middle.

lessons.title: Rules at the Machine
lessons.mainIdea: Fingers stay behind the needle, pins come out before the foot reaches them, and the machine is off whenever hands are near the needle.
reading: A sewing machine needle moves faster than you can pull away. That sets the first rule: keep your fingers at least an inch behind the presser foot, and guide the fabric from the sides, not the front. Never push fabric into the needle from in front of the foot. Let the feed dogs do the pulling; your hands only steer. Tie back long hair, remove dangling bracelets, and keep sleeves off the wheel.

Pins are the second hazard. Pin across the seam line, not along it, so the pin heads stick out to the right and are easy to grab. Pull each pin out just before the presser foot reaches it. Sewing over a pin can snap the needle, and a needle fragment flies at eye level. If the needle does break, turn the machine off, find every piece, and drop them in the sharps container.

Turn the machine off, or at least take your foot off the pedal, whenever your hands go near the needle: threading, changing the needle, changing the foot, clearing a jam. Never leave a foot resting on the pedal while you talk. Unplug the machine before you open it to clean. Keep the cord where nobody trips over it, and keep drinks off the sewing table, because a spill in a machine is a repair bill.

Work at a steady, moderate speed. Beginners who floor the pedal lose control of the seam and their hands drift toward the needle. If something goes wrong, stop; take your foot off the pedal before you lift your hands to investigate. Sewing is a calm skill. The machine only bites people who rush it.

words.d: a lidded, puncture-proof box for broken needles, bent pins and old blades
placing pins at a right angle to the seam line so they can be pulled out as the foot approaches
the habit of lifting your foot whenever your hands go near the needle

look.title: Spot the Hazards
look.text: A student sits at a machine with a water bottle on the table beside it. Her long hair hangs forward over the needle area. Pins run along the seam line, parallel to the edge, and she is sewing straight over them at full speed. Her left hand is in front of the presser foot, pushing the fabric toward the needle. A friend calls her name and she turns to talk with her foot still on the pedal.
look.prompt: List every unsafe thing in the scene, and for each say what could happen and what she should do instead.

check.q: Where should your fingers be while the machine is running?
choices: In front of the presser foot, pushing the fabric in
Behind and beside the presser foot, steering only
check.why: The feed dogs move the fabric. Hands stay behind and to the sides of the foot to steer, never in front of the needle.

check.q: Why should you pull out each pin before the foot reaches it?
choices: Pins slow down the feed dogs
Sewing over a pin can snap the needle and send a fragment flying
check.why: A needle that hits a pin can break, and the broken tip flies at eye height. Remove pins as the foot approaches.

check.q: What do you do before changing the needle or clearing a jam?
choices: Turn the machine off and take your foot off the pedal
check.why: The machine must not be able to start while hands are near the needle. Off, foot away from the pedal, then work.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Oiling
lessons.mainIdea: Lint builds up under the throat plate with every seam, and a machine brushed out and, if the manual says so, oiled regularly keeps stitching evenly for decades.
reading: Every stitch shaves a little fluff off the thread and the fabric, and it collects under the throat plate around the feed dogs and the bobbin. Enough *lint* there stops the bobbin thread from feeding smoothly and can make a well-threaded machine skip or jam. Cleaning is simple. Unplug the machine. Remove the needle and the presser foot, take out the bobbin, and unscrew or unclip the throat plate.

Use the small stiff brush that came with the machine to sweep lint out of the feed dogs and the bobbin area. Tweezers reach the stubborn bits. Do not blow into the machine; breath is damp and pushes lint deeper. Canned air pushes lint into the works too, so most manuals say brush, do not blow. Wipe the plate and the bobbin case with a dry cloth, put everything back, and turn the hand wheel a full turn by hand to make sure nothing binds.

Some machines need *oil*; many newer ones do not, so check the manual. If yours does, use only sewing machine oil, never household oil or cooking oil, which gum up. Put one drop on the spots the manual marks, usually in the hook race where the hook spins, then sew a few lines on a scrap to carry off any extra so it does not stain your project.

Cover the machine when it is not in use so dust does not settle into it. Change the needle regularly. Once a year or so, a sewing machine shop can service it fully. A well-cared-for machine from fifty years ago still sews a perfect seam; the ones that die are the ones nobody ever cleaned.

words.d: the fluff that thread and fabric shed while sewing; it gathers around the feed dogs and bobbin
the clear, light oil made for machines; household or cooking oils gum up the works
the track the hook spins in around the bobbin; the usual spot that takes one drop of oil

look.title: The Cleaning Kit and the Order
look.text: On the table: a small stiff brush, tweezers, a screwdriver for the throat plate, a dry cloth, a bottle of sewing machine oil, a can of compressed air, and a bottle of cooking spray somebody brought from home. Steps to arrange: brush the feed dogs; remove the throat plate; unplug the machine; take out the bobbin and needle; oil one drop if the manual says; sew on a scrap; reassemble.
look.prompt: Put the steps in order, and say which two items on the table should not be used on the machine and why.

check.q: What is the very first step before cleaning inside the machine?
check.why: Hands go near the needle and moving parts, so the machine must be unplugged, not just switched off.

check.q: Which tool should you use to remove lint from around the feed dogs?
choices: The small stiff brush that came with the machine
check.why: A brush lifts lint out. Blowing, by breath or by can, pushes lint and moisture deeper into the machine.

check.q: If a machine needs oil, which oil is correct?
check.why: Sewing machine oil is light and clear. Other oils thicken and gum up the works over time.

review.q: Which part pulls the top thread tight on every stitch?
review.why: The take-up lever rises with each stitch and pulls the slack out of the top thread so the lock sits in the fabric.

review.q: A student threads the machine with the presser foot down. What is the likely result?
choices: The thread misses the tension discs and loops appear underneath
review.why: The discs are closed with the foot down, so the thread never seats between them and has no tension. Loose loops form on the bottom.

review.q: Which needle size and type suits heavy denim?
review.why: Thick fabric needs a thick, sharp needle. A 100/16 denim needle pierces the layers without bending.

review.q: What does the hook do in forming a lockstitch?
choices: Catches the loop of top thread and carries it around the bobbin
Cuts the thread at the end of a seam
review.why: The hook spins around the bobbin, catches the loop that forms behind the rising needle and wraps it around the bobbin thread.

review.q: For a temporary seam that will be pulled out later, what stitch length is best?
review.why: Basting uses a long stitch so the thread slides out easily. Short stitches are hard to remove.

review.q: Dots of bobbin thread appear on the top side of the seam. Which is true?
choices: The top thread is too loose
The top thread is too tight
review.why: Too much top tension drags the bobbin thread up to the surface. Lower the top tension after checking the threading.

review.q: Which of these is the safe way to handle pins while machine sewing?
choices: Pin across the seam and pull each pin out before the foot reaches it
Pin along the seam and sew over them at speed
Leave pins in and remove them all at the end
review.why: Pins set across the seam are easy to pull as the foot approaches. Sewing over a pin can snap the needle.

review.q: The machine stitches unevenly after weeks of use, and it is threaded correctly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The foot pedal is worn out
Lint under the throat plate and around the bobbin
The stitch width is set too high
review.why: Lint builds up with every seam and interferes with the bobbin thread. Unplug, remove the plate and brush it out.

chapters.title: Seams, Corners and a First Project
chapters.bigQuestion: What has to happen at the start, the corner and the end of a seam for a bag to come out square, strong and flat?

story.title: One Perfect Corner
story.kicker: Marcus's first bag had one good corner and one that looked like a dog's ear. The difference was a single lifted foot.
paragraphs: The first real project was a drawstring bag: two rectangles of cotton, one long seam around three sides, a folded channel at the top and a cord. Marcus picked a dark green print and cut his two pieces 10 inches wide and 13 inches tall. Ms. Delgado checked his pins. "Across the seam, heads out. Good. Now find the 5/8 line on the plate and keep the edge of your fabric on it the whole way."

Marcus lined up the edge, lowered the presser foot, and sewed three stitches forward and three back to lock the start. The first side went fine. He watched the fabric edge against the line and not the needle, the way she had said, and the seam stayed straight. Then he reached the bottom corner and kept sewing, curving the fabric around the needle like steering a car. The seam came out rounded and lumpy, with a gap where the two lines of stitching did not quite meet.

"Stop there," Ms. Delgado said. "Turn the hand wheel until the needle is down in the fabric. Now lift the presser foot." With the needle holding the fabric in place like a pin, Marcus swung the bag a quarter turn. The new edge lined up on the 5/8 line by itself. "Foot down. Sew." The second corner came out sharp as a folded piece of paper.

He ripped out the first corner, resewed it with a pivot, and finished the bottom and the other side. Then came the part he had not expected: pressing. "A seam is not done until it is pressed," Ms. Delgado said. He pressed the seam flat to set the stitches, then opened it and pressed it again from the wrong side, and suddenly the bag lay flat and looked like something from a store.

The casing at the top was two folds and one more line of stitching, and threading the cord through with a safety pin took longer than sewing the whole thing. When Marcus pulled the cord and the top of the bag gathered shut, the class applauded. He looked at both corners. You could not tell which one had been sewn twice.
story.think: Marcus tried to steer around the corner while the machine was running. Why did that make a rounded, gapped corner, and what does putting the needle down before lifting the foot change?

lessons.title: The 5/8-Inch Guide
lessons.mainIdea: Seam allowance is the strip between the stitching and the raw edge; keep the fabric edge on the 5/8-inch line of the throat plate and the seam comes out straight and the right width.
reading: A seam is two pieces of fabric stitched together, and the *seam allowance* is the fabric between that line of stitching and the cut edge. Most commercial patterns for garments and home projects use a 5/8-inch seam allowance, which is about 1.5 cm. Quilting uses 1/4 inch. The pattern tells you which, and every seam in the project uses the same one, or the pieces will not fit together at the end.

Look at the *throat plate*. To the right of the needle hole are engraved lines, usually marked 3/8, 4/8 (1/2), 5/8 and 6/8. Those numbers are the distance from the needle. Put the raw edge of your fabric on the 5/8 line and your stitching lands exactly 5/8 inch in. If your plate is unmarked, measure 5/8 inch from the needle with a ruler and lay a strip of masking tape there as your guide.

Here is the habit that makes straight seams: watch the edge of the fabric against the guide line, not the needle. Beginners stare at the needle and the seam wanders. Keep your eyes an inch or two ahead of the foot, on the line, and steer the fabric with light fingertips so the edge rides along it. Let the feed dogs move the fabric. If you push or pull, the stitches stretch or bunch.

Check a finished seam with a seam gauge or ruler: measure from the stitching to the edge at three places. If it reads 5/8 at every point, the pieces will match the pattern. If it drifts from 1/2 to 3/4, the seam is uneven and the next piece will not line up. Practice on lined paper with no thread until the line stays straight, then on scraps.

words.d: the fabric between the stitching line and the cut edge; 5/8 inch on most patterns, 1/4 inch in quilting
the metal plate under the presser foot with the needle hole and engraved seam-width lines
a small ruler with a sliding marker used to check seam allowances and hems

look.title: Seam Allowances by Use (standard figures)
look.cite: standard pattern conventions; the pattern instructions always state which one to use
look.prompt: A student sews a pattern that calls for 5/8 inch at the 3/8 line. How much wider does each piece end up, and what happens when two such pieces meet a piece sewn correctly?

check.q: What is the seam allowance on most commercial garment patterns?
check.why: 5/8 inch, about 1.5 cm, is the standard on most garment and home-sewing patterns. Quilting uses 1/4 inch.

check.q: Where should your eyes be while sewing a straight seam?
choices: On the fabric edge against the guide line, just ahead of the foot
check.why: Watching the edge against the plate line keeps the seam straight. Watching the needle makes it wander.

check.q: A finished seam measures 1/2 inch at one end and 3/4 inch at the other. What is wrong?
choices: The stitch length was too short
The fabric edge drifted off the guide line
check.why: An uneven seam allowance means the raw edge moved on and off the guide line. The piece will not match the next one.

lessons.title: Start, Backstitch, End
lessons.mainIdea: Every seam starts and ends with three or four backstitches, sewn on the fabric with the tails held behind the foot, so it cannot pull open.
reading: Sit down with the machine threaded, both thread tails pulled back behind the presser foot, and the needle in its highest position. Place the fabric under the foot so the raw edge is on the 5/8 line and the needle is about 1/4 inch in from the starting edge, on the fabric, not hanging off it. Lower the presser foot. Hold the two tails lightly with your left hand behind the foot for the first few stitches so they cannot get sucked down into the plate.

Sew three or four stitches forward. Then press and hold the reverse lever or button and sew three or four stitches back over them. Release it and sew forward again, on top of the same line, and continue down the seam. That is a *backstitch*: a small knot of stitching over itself that locks the seam start. Without it, the thread ends are loose and the first inch of the seam can unravel the first time it is tugged.

At the end of the seam, sew to within a few stitches of the edge, then backstitch three or four again and stop. Turn the hand wheel toward you until the needle and the take-up lever are at their highest point; if you stop with the lever low, the thread pulls out of the needle when you move the fabric. Raise the presser foot, slide the fabric out to the back and left, and cut the threads, leaving tails of a couple of inches on the machine for the next seam.

Two mistakes to avoid: starting with the needle off the edge of the fabric, which lets the machine chew the thread into a nest under the plate, and forgetting the backstitch at the end, which is where a bag or a hem always starts to open. If you are basting a seam that will be pulled out later, skip the backstitch on purpose so it removes easily.

words.d: three or four stitches sewn in reverse over the start or end of a seam to lock it
the lever or button that makes the feed dogs move the fabric backward while it is held
the loose ends of top and bobbin thread, held behind the foot when a seam starts

look.title: Why the Seam Opened
look.text: A tote bag came back from its first day of use with the bottom seam opened for about two inches at one end. The stitching itself is fine and even; the thread simply pulled out from the end where the seam began. The sewer says she used the right seam allowance and the right tension.
look.prompt: What single step did she skip, where in the seam did it matter, and what would you tell her to do differently at the start and the end?

check.q: How do you lock the beginning of a seam?
choices: Tie the tails in a knot
Sew the first inch at stitch length 0
Sew a few stitches forward, then a few in reverse, then forward again
check.why: Backstitching three or four stitches over the start locks the thread so the seam cannot pull open.

check.q: Why should the needle start on the fabric, about 1/4 inch in, rather than off the edge?
choices: So the thread does not get pulled down into the plate and nest
So the feed dogs stay still
check.why: If the needle starts in empty space, the thread can be chewed down into the throat plate and form a tangle.

check.q: When you stop at the end of a seam, where should the take-up lever be before you pull the fabric out?
check.why: With the lever high, the thread has slack. If it is low, moving the fabric pulls the thread out of the needle.

lessons.title: Pivoting a Corner
lessons.mainIdea: To turn a sharp corner, stop with the needle down in the fabric, lift the presser foot, turn the fabric, lower the foot and go on.
reading: A square corner on a bag or a pillow is sewn with a *pivot*, not by steering around the bend while the machine runs. Sew along the first side with the edge on the 5/8 line. As you approach the corner, slow down. You need to stop exactly 5/8 inch from the end of the fabric, where the two seam lines cross. Many sewers draw a small pencil dot at that point on the wrong side before they begin.

Stop with the needle down in the fabric at the dot. If the needle stopped up, turn the hand wheel toward you until it goes down. Now the needle is holding the fabric like a pin, so it cannot slip. Lift the presser foot. Turn the fabric a quarter turn so the next raw edge lines up on the 5/8 line. Lower the foot. Sew on. The corner is exactly square and the two seam lines meet at one point.

For a very sharp point, such as the tip of a collar, take one stitch across the corner instead of a hard pivot: pivot, sew one stitch, pivot again. That one diagonal stitch gives the seam allowance room to turn without bunching at the tip. Then, before turning the piece right side out, trim the corner: cut the seam allowance off diagonally, close to but not through the stitching, so the corner turns crisp instead of lumpy.

Common mistakes: lifting the foot with the needle up, which lets the fabric slip so the seam lines miss each other; pivoting too early or too late, which makes a corner that is not square; and forgetting to lower the foot again, which sews with no pressure and produces loose, wandering stitches. A pin can hold the corner while you learn, but the needle-down habit is the one to build.

words.d: turning the fabric at a corner with the needle down and the presser foot lifted
the needle stopped inside the fabric, holding it in place while the foot is raised
cutting the seam allowance off diagonally at a corner so it turns right side out without bulk

look.title: Order the Pivot
look.text: Five steps, scrambled: (a) lower the presser foot and continue sewing; (b) turn the fabric a quarter turn so the new edge is on the guide line; (c) lift the presser foot; (d) stop 5/8 inch from the end of the fabric; (e) turn the hand wheel until the needle is down in the fabric.
look.prompt: Write the steps in order, and say what goes wrong if (c) is done before (e).

check.q: Before lifting the presser foot to turn a corner, where must the needle be?
check.why: With the needle down, the fabric is pinned in place and cannot slip while you turn it.

check.q: You lifted the foot with the needle up, turned, and sewed on. What happened to the corner?
choices: The fabric shifted and the two seam lines did not meet
check.why: Nothing held the fabric while it was turned, so the second seam line started in the wrong place.

check.q: Why trim the seam allowance diagonally at a corner before turning a bag right side out?
choices: So the corner turns crisp without a lump of fabric inside
check.why: Extra seam allowance packed into a corner makes it round and lumpy. Trimming it, close to but not through the stitching, lets the corner turn square.

lessons.title: Finishing the Raw Edge
lessons.mainIdea: Woven fabric frays at a cut edge, so seam allowances get a finish: zigzagged, pinked, serged or turned under.
reading: Cut a strip of woven cotton and rub the edge between your fingers. Threads pull loose. Every wash pulls more, and an unfinished seam allowance inside a bag or a garment slowly *frays* until the seam itself lets go. A *seam finish* is anything that stops the raw edge from fraying. The right one depends on the fabric, the machine you have and how much wear the piece will get.

The finish every machine can do is the zigzag. Set a medium zigzag, about 3 mm wide and 2 mm long, and sew along each seam allowance edge so the needle swings just over the raw edge on the right-hand side. The thread wraps the edge and holds the loose fibers. Do this before sewing the seam, on each piece separately, or after, on each side of the seam allowance. A tighter overcast stitch, if the machine has one, works the same way.

*Pinking* is the fastest finish. Pinking shears cut a zigzag edge, and the short diagonal cuts fray far less than a straight edge. It suits firm cottons that will not get heavy wear, and it is not enough for loosely woven fabric. A *serger*, also called an overlock machine, trims the edge and wraps it in three or four threads in one pass; it is the finish inside most store-bought clothes. A clean finish turns the edge under 1/4 inch and stitches it down, which is neat on light fabric.

Whatever you choose, do it before pressing and before the piece is assembled where you cannot reach the edges. For a drawstring bag, zigzag all four raw edges of both rectangles before you sew anything, and the inside of the bag will look as tidy as the outside. Skip the finish on a felt or fleece project; those fabrics do not fray.

words.d: to lose threads from a cut edge; woven fabric frays with every wash and every tug
any treatment of a raw seam-allowance edge that stops it from fraying
cutting an edge in a zigzag with pinking shears so it frays much less
an overlock machine that trims the edge and wraps it in threads in one pass

look.title: Choose the Finish
look.text: Four projects: (1) a fleece scarf; (2) a quilting-cotton drawstring bag that will be washed often; (3) a loosely woven linen tote; (4) a firm cotton wall hanging that will never be washed. The classroom has ordinary machines with a zigzag, one pair of pinking shears, and no serger.
look.prompt: Pick a finish for each project, or none, and give the one-sentence reason for each choice.

check.q: Which seam finish can be done on any basic sewing machine?
choices: A zigzag along the raw edge
A bound edge with bias tape only
check.why: A medium zigzag over the raw edge wraps the loose fibers and stops fraying, and every zigzag machine can do it.

check.q: Which fabric does NOT need a seam finish?
check.why: Fleece and felt do not fray, so their raw edges can be left as cut. Woven fabrics fray and need a finish.

check.q: When should you zigzag the edges of a drawstring bag's rectangles?
choices: Before sewing the seams, while all edges are easy to reach
Only if the bag frays later
check.why: Finishing flat pieces first is easy; once the bag is sewn, the inside edges are hard to reach.

lessons.title: Pressing Seams Open
lessons.mainIdea: Pressing means lifting and setting the iron, not sliding it; press every seam flat, then open, before sewing anything across it.
reading: Sewers say "press," not "iron," and they mean it. *Ironing* slides the iron back and forth over finished cloth to remove wrinkles. *Pressing* lifts the iron, sets it down on one spot for a few seconds, lifts it again and moves to the next spot. Sliding stretches a freshly sewn seam and pushes it off grain. Pressing flattens it exactly where it lies. Set up the iron at the temperature for your fiber: high for cotton and linen, medium for wool, low for polyester and nylon. When in doubt, test on a scrap.

First, *set the stitches*: lay the seam flat, still closed, and press right along the stitching line. This sinks the thread into the fabric and evens the tension. Second, open the seam. Lay the piece wrong side up and use your fingers to spread the two seam allowances apart, one to each side. Press down the center of the open seam with the point of the iron, moving along in short lifts. Third, turn the piece over and press lightly from the right side, with a *press cloth* between the iron and the fabric if it is dark or shiny.

Steam helps set cotton and linen; a burst from the iron or a damp press cloth makes the seam lie flatter. Skip steam on fabrics the care label says to keep dry. For a seam that is pressed to one side instead of open, such as a quilt seam, press both allowances toward the darker fabric so they do not show through.

The rule is: press every seam before you sew across it. A side seam gets pressed open before the casing goes on. A seam that is crossed while still folded leaves a lump that no amount of pressing fixes later. Keep the iron on its heel when your hands are off it, keep the cord away from the machine, and never leave a hot iron face down on the board.

words.d: lifting the iron and setting it down on one spot, then lifting and moving, so the fabric does not stretch
sliding the iron across cloth to remove wrinkles; not used on fresh seams
pressing along the closed seam line first so the thread sinks into the fabric
a piece of thin cotton laid between the iron and the fabric to protect dark or shiny cloth

look.title: Two Pressing Sessions
look.text: Student A sets the iron to cotton, presses along the closed seam, opens it with her fingers, presses down the center from the wrong side in lifts, then flips it and presses lightly through a press cloth. Student B sets the iron to the hottest setting for a polyester blend, slides it back and forth over the open seam from the right side, and leaves the iron face down while she pins the next piece.
look.prompt: List each thing Student B did that Student A did not, and say what each one risks.

check.q: What is the difference between pressing and ironing?
choices: Pressing lifts and sets the iron; ironing slides it
Pressing uses steam; ironing does not
check.why: Pressing lifts the iron and sets it down in one spot. Sliding stretches fresh seams and pushes fabric off grain.

check.q: What does "set the stitches" mean?
choices: Sew the seam a second time
Press along the closed seam line before opening it
Turn the stitch length dial to a fixed number
check.why: Pressing the closed seam first sinks the thread into the fabric and evens the tension before the seam is opened.

check.q: Why press a side seam open before sewing the casing across the top of it?
choices: So the thread does not break
So the seam finish stays put
So the bobbin does not run out
So no folded lump gets sewn into the casing
check.why: A seam crossed while still folded leaves a permanent lump. Pressing it open first keeps the crossing flat.

lessons.title: Plan, Measure and Cut
lessons.mainIdea: A drawstring bag starts as two rectangles cut on grain, with a plan that already accounts for seam allowance and the casing fold.
reading: Before you cut, decide on the finished size and work backward. Suppose you want a bag about 8¾ inches wide and 11 inches tall, big enough for gym shoes. Each side seam takes 5/8 inch, so add 1¼ inches to the width: cut 10 inches wide. The top casing takes a ½-inch fold plus a 1¼-inch fold, and the bottom seam takes 5/8 inch, so add about 2½ inches to the height: cut 13 inches tall. Two rectangles, 10 by 13 inches each. Write the numbers on your plan.

Wash and dry the fabric first if the bag will be washed, so it shrinks before you sew, not after. Press it. Find the *grain*: the lengthwise threads run parallel to the finished edge, called the selvage. Lay the rectangles so the 13-inch side runs along the grain; a bag cut off grain twists after washing. Measure with a clear ruler or tape, mark the cutting lines with chalk or a washable marker on the wrong side, and check every measurement twice.

Cut with sharp fabric shears, taking long strokes and keeping the lower blade flat on the table. Do not lift the fabric into the air as you cut, or the line wanders. If you have a rotary cutter and mat, use a ruler as a guide and keep fingers well back from the blade. Zigzag all four edges of both pieces now, while they are flat.

Last, gather the notions: matching thread, two cords or lengths of ribbon about 30 inches each, a large safety pin for threading the cord, and pins. Make a short step list with the seam allowance written at the top. Cutting is the one step you cannot undo, so the plan gets checked before the shears come out.

words.d: the direction of the lengthwise threads in woven fabric, parallel to the selvage
the tightly woven finished edge along each side of a bolt of fabric
the small supplies a project needs besides fabric: thread, cord, pins, buttons, zippers
a folded and stitched channel at the top of a bag that a drawstring runs through

look.title: Cutting Plan for One Bag (example)
look.cite: example figures for a shoe-bag-size project; adjust for your own size
look.prompt: Check the arithmetic: does 10 inches minus two 5/8-inch seams give 8¾? Then plan the cut size for a bag 12 inches wide finished.

check.q: Why do the rectangles get cut wider than the finished bag?
choices: To allow 5/8 inch for each side seam
check.why: Each side seam uses 5/8 inch of fabric. Two seams take 1¼ inches, so a 10-inch cut gives an 8¾-inch bag.

check.q: Why wash the fabric before cutting a bag that will be laundered?
choices: To make it easier to pin
So it shrinks before the bag is sewn, not after
check.why: Cotton can shrink in the first wash. Prewashing means the finished bag keeps its size and shape.

check.q: What does cutting "on grain" mean?
choices: Lining the long side of the piece up with the lengthwise threads, parallel to the selvage
Cutting only with a rotary cutter
Cutting from the right side of the fabric
check.why: On-grain pieces run with the lengthwise threads. Off-grain pieces twist and hang crooked after washing.

lessons.title: Sewing the Sides and Bottom
lessons.mainIdea: Right sides together, pinned across the seam, sewn at 5/8 inch with backstitches and pivots, and a gap left at the top of each side for the cord to come out.
reading: Lay one rectangle on the table right side up. Lay the second on top, right side down, so the two *right sides* face each other; that is how nearly every seam in sewing is made, so the seam allowance ends up inside when you turn the piece. Line up all the edges. Pin across the seam line along both long sides and the bottom, with pin heads sticking out to the right, about every three inches.

Mark the cord opening. On each side seam, measure down from the top edge and make a chalk mark at 1¾ inches; the casing will fold at ½ inch and again at 1¼, so the opening has to sit below that fold. You will sew the side seam from the bottom up to that mark and stop, leaving the top 1¾ inches of each side unsewn. That gap is where the cord will come out of the casing.

Start at the top of one side at the 1¾-inch mark, needle on the fabric, edge on the 5/8 line. Backstitch, sew down the side, pull pins as you reach them. At the bottom corner, stop with the needle down 5/8 inch from the edge, lift the foot, pivot, lower the foot, sew across the bottom. Pivot again at the second corner and sew up the other side to its 1¾-inch mark. Backstitch and stop. Trim both bottom corners diagonally.

Press the seams flat to set them, then press each side seam open from the wrong side, including the unsewn 1¾ inches at the top, which you fold under along the 5/8 line and press. Those little pressed-under flaps make a neat edge around the cord opening. Stitch around each opening close to the fold so the flaps stay put. Now the bag is a pocket with a raw top edge, ready for the casing.

words.d: placing two pieces so their printed or good sides face each other before sewing a seam
the unsewn top part of each side seam where the drawstring exits the casing
the back or plain side of a fabric, which ends up inside the finished piece

look.title: The Inside-Out Bag
look.text: A student pinned her two rectangles with the printed sides facing outward, sewed both sides and the bottom at 5/8 inch with neat backstitches and perfect pivots, and turned the bag. The seams and all their zigzagged edges are now on the outside of the bag, and the print is on the inside.
look.prompt: Name the one step that went wrong, and explain why every other step being perfect could not save the bag.

check.q: How are the two rectangles placed before sewing the seams?
choices: One on top of the other, both facing up
check.why: Right sides together puts the seam allowances inside once the bag is turned, so the print is on the outside.

check.q: Why is the top 1¾ inches of each side seam left unsewn?
choices: To make the bag wider at the top
To leave an opening where the cord comes out of the casing
Because the casing is sewn there first
check.why: The casing folds at the top; the gap below the fold is where the drawstring exits. Without it there is no way to pull the cord.

check.q: At each bottom corner of the bag, what is the correct sequence?
choices: Needle down, foot up, turn, foot down, sew
Foot up, needle down, turn, sew
Sew around the corner in a curve
Stop, cut the thread, restart on the next side
check.why: The pivot: needle down to hold the fabric, lift the foot, turn a quarter turn, lower the foot, continue.

lessons.title: The Casing and the Cord
lessons.mainIdea: The casing is a double fold at the top, stitched close to the lower fold, and the cords go through it with a safety pin from opposite sides.
reading: With the bag still wrong side out, fold the top raw edge down ½ inch toward the wrong side all the way around and press. Fold again 1¼ inches and press. The raw edge is now hidden inside the fold, and the pressed-under flaps at the cord openings sit inside the fold too. Pin the fold across, every couple of inches, with the heads out.

Turn the bag so you can sew around the inside of the top. Sew close to the lower folded edge, about 1/8 inch from it, all the way around, removing pins as you go. Backstitch where you start and where you meet your starting point. This stitching line closes the casing; the space between it and the top fold is the *channel* the cord runs through. Check that the two side openings are above the stitching and open into the channel.

Cut two cords about 30 inches long. Pin a large *safety pin* through one end of the first cord and push it into the left opening. Scrunch the fabric along the pin and pull it through, all the way around the bag and back out the same opening. Tie the two ends together. Do the second cord from the right opening the same way and tie it. Now pulling both knots in opposite directions closes the bag.

Turn the bag right side out, poke the corners square with a blunt tool such as a chopstick, and give it a final press. Then evaluate: measure the finished width and height against your plan, check that every seam is 5/8, look inside for raw edges, and test the drawstring ten times. Write down what you would change on the next one. A bag that closes, holds its shape and has no loose threads is a pass.

words.d: the space inside the casing, between the top fold and the stitching line, that the cord runs through
the tool pinned to the end of a cord to push and pull it through a casing
folding an edge under once to hide the raw edge, then again to make the casing

look.title: A Casing That Will Not Take a Cord
look.text: A finished bag looks good, but the safety pin stops an inch into the casing every time. Looking closely: the casing was folded ½ inch and then 1¼ inches, and the stitching runs 1/8 inch from the lower fold. But at one side seam, the unsewn opening was pressed and stitched shut, and at the other, the casing stitching was sewn 1 inch from the fold instead of 1/8 inch.
look.prompt: Explain what each mistake did to the channel, and say which one can be fixed with a seam ripper alone.

check.q: Where does the casing stitching go?
choices: Down the center of the casing
About 1/8 inch from the lower folded edge, all the way around
check.why: Stitching close to the lower fold closes the casing and leaves the widest possible channel above it for the cord.

check.q: Why does the top edge get folded ½ inch first and then 1¼ inches?
choices: So the raw edge is hidden inside the second fold
check.why: The first small fold tucks the raw edge inside. The second fold makes the channel. A single fold would leave a fraying edge.

check.q: How do you get the cord through the casing?
choices: Sew the cord in as you stitch the casing
Pin a safety pin to the end and work it through the channel
Push it with the point of the scissors
check.why: A safety pin gives you something to grip and push. Scrunch the fabric along it and pull it through the opening and around.

lessons.title: Skipped Stitches
lessons.mainIdea: Skipped stitches almost always come from the needle: dull, bent, the wrong type for the fabric, or not pushed all the way up when inserted.
reading: A seam with *skipped stitches* has long gaps where a stitch should be, then a few good stitches, then another gap. The hook is missing the loop on some strokes. Because the loop forms next to the needle, the needle is the first suspect. Turn the machine off. Take the needle out and roll it on the table; a bent one wobbles. Run a fingertip along the point; a dull or burred one catches. Either way, throw it in the sharps box and put in a fresh one.

Second suspect: the wrong needle for the fabric. A universal needle on a stretchy knit pushes the loops aside and skips; a ballpoint fixes it. A fine needle on thick denim flexes and skips; a 100/16 denim needle fixes it. Third: the needle is in wrong. It must be pushed all the way up into the clamp with the flat side to the back and the screw tightened firmly. A needle that sits 1/16 inch low puts the loop out of the hook's reach.

Fourth: threading. Pull the top thread out and rethread with the presser foot up, making sure the thread goes through every guide and the take-up lever, and that the needle is threaded front to back. Fifth: thread and needle mismatch. Very thick thread in a small needle cannot form a clean loop. Use ordinary all-purpose thread for class projects and the needle size the fabric calls for.

Work down the list in order and test on a scrap after each step. Most of the time the first or second step ends it. If a fresh, correct needle, correctly inserted and threaded, still skips, the machine's timing may be off, and that is a repair-shop job, not a classroom one. Tell the teacher and switch machines.

words.d: a tiny rough spot on a needle point, often from hitting a pin, that snags thread and fabric
the precise relationship between the needle's position and the hook's; only a technician adjusts it
ordinary polyester or cotton-wrapped polyester thread that suits most fabrics and needle sizes

look.title: Work the Checklist
look.text: A student sewing a fleece pouch gets a stitch, a gap, two stitches, a gap. She is using the universal 80/12 needle that was in the machine when she sat down, threaded front to back with the foot up, all-purpose thread. She rolls the needle on the table and it looks straight.
look.prompt: Which step of the checklist is most likely to solve it, and why does the straight needle not rule out the needle as the problem?

check.q: A seam has regular gaps where stitches are missing. What is the first thing to check?
choices: The needle: bent, dull or wrong type
check.why: Skipped stitches mean the hook missed the loop, and the loop forms at the needle. Replace or correct the needle first.

check.q: A universal needle skips on T-shirt knit. What is the fix?
check.why: A ballpoint's rounded tip slides between knit loops instead of pushing them aside, so the loop forms and the hook catches it.

check.q: A fresh, correct needle, fully inserted and correctly threaded, still skips on every fabric. What should the student do?
choices: Tell the teacher; the timing may need a technician
check.why: Once the needle and threading are ruled out, skipped stitches point to timing, which is a repair-shop adjustment.

lessons.title: Nests, Jams and Puckers
lessons.mainIdea: A thread nest under the fabric comes from the top thread, a jam from the bobbin area or lint, and a pucker from tension or stitch length; each has its own short checklist.
reading: The classic beginner's disaster is the *thread nest*: a wad of loops under the fabric and a machine that stops with a thunk. Surprisingly, a nest on the bottom is almost always a top-thread problem. Either the machine was threaded with the presser foot down, so the thread never seated in the tension discs, or the foot was left up while sewing, so there was no tension at all, or the tails were not held at the start and got pulled down. Cut the fabric free, clear every scrap of thread from the bobbin area, and rethread the top with the foot up.

If the machine sews a few inches and then binds, or the bobbin thread keeps breaking, look under the plate. Check that the bobbin is the right one, in the right way round, with its thread under the spring. Check for lint packed around the feed dogs and hook, and brush it out. Check that there is no thread wrapped around the hook. Turn the hand wheel by hand a full turn; if it turns freely, you are ready to try again on a scrap.

If the fabric will not move, the presser foot is probably up, the feed dogs may be lowered by the darning switch, or the stitch length may be at zero. If the seam *puckers*, drawing the fabric up into little ridges, the top tension is too tight, the needle is too big or dull for a fine fabric, or the stitch is too long for it; try a smaller needle and a shorter stitch, and lower the tension one step. Pulling the fabric through by hand also puckers and can bend the needle.

Make yourself a card for the machine: nest underneath, rethread top with foot up. Jam or breaking bobbin thread, check bobbin and lint. Fabric will not feed, foot, feed dogs, length. Pucker, tension, needle, length. Every fix begins with the machine off and the foot off the pedal, and every fix ends with a test on a scrap before you touch the project again.

words.d: a tangle of loops under the fabric; usually a top-thread problem, not a bobbin one
small ridges along a seam where the fabric has been drawn up by tight tension or a wrong needle
the control that lowers the feed dogs for free-motion work; if left on, fabric will not feed

look.title: Three Machines, Three Complaints
look.text: Machine 1: sews fine on top but leaves a wad of loops underneath, and the presser foot lever was found up. Machine 2: the fabric just sits there while the needle goes up and down; the stitch length dial reads 0. Machine 3: the seam draws the fine cotton up into ridges; the tension dial is at 8 and the needle is a 100/16.
look.prompt: Give the cause and the fix for each machine, and say which of the three needs nothing more than a lever.

check.q: There is a nest of loops under the fabric. Where is the problem most likely?
choices: The top thread: not seated in the tension discs or the foot left up
check.why: Loops underneath mean the top thread has no tension. Rethread with the foot up and sew with the foot down.

check.q: The needle moves but the fabric does not. Which is a likely cause?
choices: The presser foot is up or the stitch length is at 0
check.why: The feed dogs need the foot's pressure and a stitch length above zero to move fabric. A lowered feed-dog switch has the same effect.

check.q: A seam on fine cotton puckers into ridges. Which change is right?
choices: Lower the tension one step and use a smaller needle and shorter stitch
Raise the tension and use a bigger needle
Switch to a 4 mm basting stitch
check.why: Puckering comes from tension that is too tight, a needle too big for the fabric, or stitches too long. Lighten all three.

review.q: What is the standard seam allowance on most commercial patterns, and where do you find its guide on the machine?
choices: 5/8 inch, on the engraved lines of the throat plate
review.why: 5/8 inch is the standard. The throat plate's engraved lines measure from the needle, so the fabric edge rides on the 5/8 line.

review.q: What locks the start and end of a seam?
choices: A knot tied in the tails
review.why: Backstitching sews over the first and last stitches in reverse, so the seam cannot pull open.

review.q: To turn a square corner, the order is:
choices: Foot up, turn, needle down, sew
Needle down, foot up, turn, foot down, sew
review.why: The needle holds the fabric while the foot is lifted for the turn. Foot down again before sewing.

review.q: Which finish stops a woven seam allowance from fraying using only a basic machine?
choices: A straight stitch 1/8 inch from the edge
A medium zigzag over the raw edge
Nothing; woven fabric does not fray
review.why: A zigzag wraps the raw edge in thread. Pressing and straight stitching do not hold loose fibers.

review.q: What is wrong with sliding the iron back and forth over a fresh seam?
choices: It stretches the seam and pushes the fabric off grain
review.why: Pressing lifts and sets the iron. Sliding stretches a freshly sewn seam; the fabric distorts.

review.q: A drawstring bag's rectangles are cut 10 inches wide with 5/8-inch seams. How wide is the finished bag?
review.why: Two side seams use 1¼ inches total. 10 minus 1¼ is 8¾ inches.

review.q: The seams of a finished bag are on the outside and the print is inside. What went wrong?
choices: The stitch length was too short
The pieces were sewn wrong sides together instead of right sides together
The bag was pressed too hot
review.why: Seams are sewn with right sides together so the allowances end up inside when the piece is turned.

review.q: Skipped stitches appear on a knit fabric with a universal needle. What is the most likely fix?
review.why: Knits need a ballpoint needle so the loop forms properly and the hook catches it. Universal points push the loops aside and skip.
